original_question: For the graph (V,E) of the Penrose tiling, consider the operator H on l^2(V) defined by [Hψ](v)=sum_{w:(v,w) in E}(ψ(w)-ψ(v)). Determine the spectrum σ(H) of this operator.
target_in_paper: Section 2.1, Problem 2.1.2: determine the spectrum of the operator on the Penrose-tiling graph defined by [Hψ](v)=sum_{w:(v,w)∈E}(ψ(w)-ψ(v)).
correct_elements: Your draft is essentially a near-verbatim restatement of the paper’s actual problem. It correctly identifies the Penrose tiling graph, uses the same operator H on l^2(V) with the same formula, and asks for the spectrum σ(H), which is exactly what Problem 2.1.2 asks.
missing_details: Make explicit that V is the vertex set and E is the edge set of the graph corresponding to the Penrose tiling.
State the quantifiers in the operator definition: H is defined for every ψ∈l^2(V) and every v∈V.
Specify the ambient Hilbert space as the usual complex l^2(V) of square-summable functions on V.
Avoid adding stronger goals not present in the paper, such as proving the spectrum is Cantor, zero-measure, or determining spectral measures; the paper’s official problem only asks to determine σ(H).
refined_question:
Consider the graph (V,E) corresponding to the Penrose tiling, where V is the vertex set and E is the set of edges. Define an operator H on the Hilbert space l^2(V) by
[Hψ](v)=∑_{w:(v,w)∈E}(ψ(w)-ψ(v))
for every ψ∈l^2(V) and every v∈V. Determine the spectrum σ(H) of H.
justification: The closest official formulation is not a conjecture or theorem but Section 2.1, Problem 2.1.2, which your draft already mirrors very closely. The surrounding context in Section 2.1 first explains that spectral questions for Schrödinger operators are central in quasicrystal models, then presents Theorem 2.1.1 as an example of the sort of spectral behavior one studies in one dimension, and only afterward states the Penrose-tiling problem in higher dimensions. So the faithful refinement should stay narrow: define exactly the same operator on the Penrose graph and ask only for σ(H), without importing the zero-Lebesgue-measure, Cantor-set, or singular-continuity conclusions from the preceding one-dimensional theorem.
